notes.meaning: Jonathan explains the secret signal that means danger. If he shoots an arrow past the boy, David will know that King Saul wants to kill him. In that case, David must flee immediately, trusting that the Lord is directing him away to safety.

Jonathan reminds David of their solemn covenant, a sacred promise of lifelong friendship. Even though danger and distance will separate them, God stands as the eternal witness between them. Both men and their descendants are bound to honor this covenant before the Lord forever.

David slips away to hide in the open field just as they planned. Meanwhile, the special monthly feast of the New Moon begins back at the palace. King Saul sits down to eat the festival meal, where his top leaders are expected to join him.

Saul sits in his customary seat of honor by the wall. Jonathan stands up out of respect, and Saul's commander Abner sits next to the king. Everyone takes their assigned place, but David's seat remains visibly empty.

Saul says nothing about David's absence on the first day. He assumes David became ceremonially unclean, which means ritually unfit under God's law to share in a holy meal. Because such uncleanness usually lasted only until evening, Saul expects David to return the next day.

On the second day of the festival, David's place at the table is still empty. Saul realizes a brief ritual uncleanness cannot explain a two-day absence. He asks Jonathan why the son of Jesse has not come to eat, using David's family name to show scorn.

Jonathan gives the excuse that he and David had agreed on earlier. He tells his father that David urgently asked permission to attend an annual family sacrifice in Bethlehem at his brother's command. Jonathan describes David as an obedient servant who asked for leave properly rather than neglecting the king's table.

Saul bursts into a violent rage against Jonathan. He uses harsh words to insult Jonathan and Jonathan's mother, accusing his son of being a stubborn rebel against his own family. Saul claims that Jonathan's close friendship with David brings public shame on himself and his royal house.

Saul warns Jonathan that as long as David lives, Jonathan will never secure his throne or become king. Saul views David purely as a dangerous rival who must be destroyed. He orders Jonathan to send for David right away so he can be executed.
Jonathan boldly challenges his father's murderous order. He asks why David deserves to die and what wrong he has committed. Jonathan refuses to let his friend be condemned without any just cause.

Saul becomes so wild with rage that he hurls his spear at his own son to kill him. Jonathan dodges the weapon and now knows with absolute certainty that his father is resolved to murder David. Any hope of softening Saul's heart is completely gone.

Jonathan leaves the feast in fierce anger and refuses to eat anything on that second day. He is deeply grieved by how shamefully and unjustly his father treated David. Saul's uncontrolled hatred ruins what should have been a sacred celebration.

The next morning, Jonathan goes out to the field at the prearranged time to send the signal to David. He brings along a young servant boy to carry his bow and arrows. A small boy would carry the gear without suspecting any hidden plan.

Jonathan tells the boy to run ahead and fetch the arrows he shoots. While the boy is running, Jonathan intentionally shoots an arrow far past him. This was the exact sign agreed upon to warn David of fatal danger.

When the boy gets near the area where the arrow landed, Jonathan calls out that the arrow lies farther ahead. The words are spoken aloud to the boy, but their true meaning is directed at David hiding in the field. The message makes it clear that Saul is determined to kill him.

Jonathan shouts after the boy to hurry and not stand still. The servant thinks his master is merely in a rush during archery practice, but Jonathan is secretly urging David to flee without delay. The boy gathers the arrow and brings it back to Jonathan.

The young helper does not suspect that anything unusual has taken place. Only Jonathan and David understand what the flight of that arrow really meant. With that single signal, David's life at court ends and his journey as a fugitive begins.

Jonathan hands his bow, arrows, and quiver to the boy and tells him to take them back to the town. Sending the servant away gives Jonathan a private moment in the open field. Seeing that the area is safe, he risks a brief personal goodbye with David.

Once the boy is gone, David comes out from the south side of his hiding rock. He bows three times with his face to the ground to honor Jonathan as the prince and the protector who saved his life. Then the two friends embrace, kiss, and weep aloud together, with David weeping even more because he is losing his home, family, and the public worship of God.

Jonathan gives David a final blessing to go in peace, resting on the sacred promise they made in the name of the Lord. They trust that God will guard their bond and protect both of their families forever, even through long separation. Then David departs to begin his life on the run, and Jonathan heads back into the city.
